title: The Curriculum

choices.label: Accept the curriculum.
choices.resultText: You fold the letter along its creases, which are exact. Under your arm the Register enters the receipt of a curriculum, and then, after some thought, the strike. 'Thorough,' it says. 'Almost.'

choices.label: Write back.
choices.resultText: You write back. Your letter comes home by the next post with two corrections in the margin and one word at the foot, where a mark would go: "Received."

choices.label: Write back: 'You are going to ask me for the proper name of what I did.'
choices.resultText: Her answer comes by the next post, on a card, in the careful script: "How". There is no mark after it at all. From Wenna Aldric, that is very nearly a shout. Under it, smaller, and in better order: "The first examination is entered as sat. Proceed to the second."

title: {exam_title}
body:
A Sending reaches you, in complete sentences, with the punctuation audible.

'I am told you won a fight. Winning is a result, and I did not ask for a result. I asked what you did. Give it its proper name.'

choices.label: 'I won.'
choices.resultText: 'That is the result,' she says. 'I asked for the act.' A pause, exactly as long as it needs to be. 'Noted.' She does not say whether you passed. {exam_followup}

choices.label: 'I ended it.'
choices.resultText: A silence on the line, the attentive kind. 'Yes,' she says. 'Winning is something that happens to you. Ending is something you do.' She does not say whether you passed. {exam_followup}

choices.label: 'I survived it.'
choices.resultText: 'You did,' she says. 'That is not nothing. It is a condition for having an answer, which is not the same as having one.' She does not say whether you passed. {exam_followup}

title: {exam_title}
body:
A Sending reaches you, in complete sentences, with the punctuation audible.

'I am told there is an agreement, and that your name is on it. What did you do to get it? Give it its proper name.'

choices.label: 'I got a good price.'
choices.resultText: 'You got a price,' she says. 'Whether it was good is for their grandchildren to decide.' She does not say whether you passed. {exam_followup}

choices.label: 'I gave them what they needed.'
choices.resultText: 'Generous,' she says, in the voice she keeps for sentences that are grammatical and wrong. 'And how did you know what they needed?' The question is not for you. She has already moved on. She does not say whether you passed. {exam_followup}

choices.label: 'I found out what they wanted, and named it before they could.'
choices.resultText: A pause. 'That is called naming,' she says. 'It is the only thing I teach.' She does not say whether you passed. {exam_followup}

title: {exam_title}
body:
A Sending reaches you, in complete sentences, with the punctuation audible.

'I am told the road asked you something and you answered. I am not interested in the question. Tell me what you did. Give it its proper name.'

choices.label: 'I chose, and now I have to keep choosing it.'
choices.resultText: The line is quiet for longer than her pauses usually last. 'Yes,' she says. 'That is the only kind of choice there is. The other kind is called an accident.' She does not say whether you passed. {exam_followup}

choices.label: 'I helped.'
choices.resultText: 'Whom?' she says, and then, before you can answer: 'No. Helped is a kind word for a great many different acts. Find out which one it was.' She does not say whether you passed. {exam_followup}

choices.label: 'I passed through.'
choices.resultText: 'Nobody passes through,' she says. 'You were changed in transit, and so was the road. Look again.' She does not say whether you passed. {exam_followup}

title: Number Fifteen
body:
Wenna Aldric has come to the edge on foot. She has set a folding desk in the road a careful hundred paces out, which is as near to her school as anyone can stand without you, and she is standing behind it.

On the desk is a list in her careful script. Seventeen lines. Fourteen are struck through. Sixteen and seventeen are written out in full. Fifteen is a number and nothing else.

'The third examination is one question,' she says. 'I have been setting it for eleven years, and nobody has sat it.' She turns the list to face you and lays one finger beside the bare number. 'What is number fifteen?'

{remembrance}

choices.label: 'I don't know.'
choices.resultText:
'Correct,' she says. 'Nobody does. I have seen to that.' She looks at the number for a long moment. 'Every year the entrance examination is easier, and every year fewer pass it. I have been lowering the bar for eleven years to keep the rooms full.' Her pen comes down toward the page and stops a finger's width above it. 'I did not want to write down why.'

Under your arm the Register has already written it down, every word, in her careful script. She watches it do so, and does not object. 'The church kept these numbers for centuries and called them holiness,' she says. 'I have called them a curriculum problem for eleven years.' She caps the pen. 'Now. The audience.'

choices.label: 'Fewer of them can learn it, every year.'
choices.resultText:
'Who told you?' she says, very sharply, and then, before you can answer: 'No. Nobody told you. You worked it out, which is worse.' She looks at the number for a long moment. 'Every year the entrance examination is easier, and every year fewer pass it. I have been lowering the bar for eleven years to keep the rooms full.' Her pen comes down toward the page and stops a finger's width above it. 'I did not want to write down why.'

Under your arm the Register has already written it down, every word, in her careful script. She watches it do so, and does not object. 'The church kept these numbers for centuries and called them holiness,' she says. 'I have called them a curriculum problem for eleven years.' She caps the pen. 'Now. The audience.'

choices.label: 'You lowered the bar. Eleven years. You never wrote down why.'
choices.resultText:
Wenna Aldric sits down, which she does not do in front of students. 'I have told no one that,' she says. 'You told me,' you say. She does not ask when. For a while she looks at you the way she looked at the bare number. 'Fewer of them can learn it every year,' she says at last. 'I did not want to write down why.'

Under your arm the Register writes your words in your hand and hers in hers, on facing lines. 'The church kept these numbers for centuries and called them holiness,' she says. 'I have called them a curriculum problem for eleven years.' She caps the pen, and stands. 'Now. The audience.'

title: One Hour
body:
You walk Wenna Aldric through the edge, and for one hour the founder of the Academy stands in her school.

She does not look at the sky, or the bell, or the feast. She goes first to the lecture rooms, where the chalkboards stopped in the middle of a morning's teaching, and she corrects them: a misplaced sign, a wrong declension, a name spelled the way students spell it. The chalk leaves no mark. She corrects them anyway, every one, in order, and does not hurry.

Last, she comes to the ceremony hall and stands at the foot of the dais. At the lectern the Wenna Aldric of that afternoon stands with her mouth open on the next word, one hand flat on the place where the Register lay. The spell hangs where it has always hung, a line of white fire an arm's length from the place where you stood, pointing past it, at her.

'It was meant for me,' she says.

She has never said it before. You can tell from the way she listens to it, all the way to the end. Under your arm the Register writes it down in her careful script, one line below the line that stops.

{remembrance}

choices.label: 'I know.'
choices.resultText: 'Of course you know,' she says. 'You were in the way.' It is as near as she will come, and you both know it. 'We will not discuss it again.' On the way out she stops at one more chalkboard, and corrects it.

choices.label: Say nothing.
choices.resultText: You say nothing, and she does not seem to need you to. When the hour is up she is waiting at the gate with her spectacles folded, and she walks out through the edge without looking back, which is how she leaves every room she means to come back to.
